blocks.text: A naive segment tree RANGE update, applying a change to every element in a range, requires visiting every leaf in that range individually, costing O(range size) in the worst case, which for a range covering the whole array degrades to O(n) per update, defeating the point of a segment tree's O(log n) promise. Lazy propagation restores O(log n) range updates by DEFERRING work rather than doing it immediately.

The core idea in one sentence: when an update fully covers a node's range, update that node's aggregate directly using a closed form formula, and store the pending change in a lazy value WITHOUT pushing it down to children until it is actually needed.

When a range update fully covers a node's range, instead of recursing all the way down to every leaf, update that node's aggregate value directly using a closed form formula. For a range add, the node's sum increases by delta times the number of elements in its range.

STORE the pending delta in a separate "lazy" value at that node without pushing it down to children yet. The children's stored aggregates become temporarily "not yet accurate," but this is fine because the pending delta is recorded, and will be applied to the children LATER, only if and when a future query or update actually needs to descend into those children.

blocks.caption: A node fully covered by a range update gets its aggregate updated directly and a lazy value stored, deferring propagation to its children.

blocks.text: Whenever a query or update needs to recurse INTO a node's children, first check if that node has a pending lazy value. If so, apply it to both children immediately, updating each child's own aggregate using the same closed form formula, and ADDING the lazy delta to each child's own lazy value rather than overwriting, since a child might already have its own pending lazy value from a previous incomplete propagation.

blocks.caption: Pushing down applies the parent's lazy delta to both children's aggregates and accumulates it into their own lazy values, then the parent's lazy value is cleared.

blocks.text: After applying to both children, clear the current node's lazy value. This way, work is only ever done exactly when needed, never before.

Applying a range add of +5 to indices 2 through 5 on an 8 element array: nodes whose range is FULLY covered by [2,5] get their aggregate updated directly (sum increases by 5 times their range size) and a lazy value of 5 is stored, without recursing into their children. Nodes completely OUTSIDE [2,5] are left entirely untouched. Nodes with PARTIAL overlap require recursing into their children, but before doing so, any existing lazy value at that node must first be pushed down.

A subsequent range SUM query that touches some of the previously lazy nodes triggers a push down at exactly the right moment: when the query recursion needs to descend past a node carrying a pending lazy value, that value is applied to the children first, keeping the result correct even though the children's aggregates were temporarily stale.

Both range update and range query run in O(log n) amortized. Each operation still only touches O(log n) "boundary" nodes directly, all further work is deferred via the lazy values and only materializes on demand, so the total work never exceeds what a query touching those nodes would have needed anyway.

blocks.text: Forgetting to push down before recursing into children during either an update OR a query, silently reads stale aggregate values that have not yet had a pending lazy delta applied.

Overwriting a child's lazy value during push down instead of ADDING to it: this loses a previous pending update that had not yet been pushed further down, silently dropping part of an earlier range update.

Forgetting to clear the parent's lazy value to 0 after pushing it down: this causes the same delta to be double applied later, since the parent would appear to still have a pending update that was already propagated.

Range Sum Query Mutable can be extended into a range update variant that specifically needs lazy propagation. Range Addition is a direct application. Falling Squares is a genuinely advanced application using lazy propagation style range max updates. This is a topic more common in competitive programming and advanced interview rounds than typical entry level interviews, but demonstrates strong mastery when it comes up.

items: Can you explain, precisely, why a naive range update degrades to O(n) and how lazy propagation restores O(log n)?
Can you implement pushDown correctly, including accumulating (not overwriting) a child's lazy value?
Can you trace a worked example where a query correctly triggers a push down at exactly the right moment?
Can you explain why clearing a node's lazy value after pushing it down is required for correctness?

description: Learn how lazy propagation defers range update work using pending lazy values and push down, restoring O(log n) range updates instead of O(range size)
title: Introduction to Segment Tree Lazy Propagation
